title: Self-Induced Stretch Syncope: An Unusual Non-Epileptic Paroxysmal Event. A Case Report and Literature Mini-Review
case_prompt:
An 8-year-old girl presented with a 5-month history of brief (5–20 sec) paroxysmal episodes of altered consciousness and postural instability, occasionally accompanied by facial grimacing, upper-limb tremors, and falls. Each event was always preceded by stereotyped head tilting against one shoulder, back and neck hyperextension, and stretching of the arms. Episodes occurred only during wakefulness, were followed by prompt and complete recovery, and increased in frequency over time. There was no family history of neurologic disorders or syncope. Two prior hospital admissions with blood chemistries, neurologic and cardiovascular assessments, and brain MRI (showing only a quadrigeminal cistern lipoma) were unremarkable; standard supra-aortic trunk and transcranial Doppler were normal.

On a 4-day video-polysomnography (EEG, electrooculography, electromyography, ECG, respiratory monitoring, oximetry), 50–100 typical events were recorded daily and could be voluntarily provoked. Each began with head tilt (more often to the right), neck hyperextension, and arm stretching, followed by a grimacing smile or behavioral arrest with variable loss of tone. During events, EEG showed bursts of monomorphic 2–3 Hz slow-wave activity lasting 3–12 sec, predominantly frontotemporal and mainly ipsilateral to the head tilt. Mild sinus tachycardia was noted; oximetry and blood pressure were not measurable due to artifacts. Provocative maneuvers including Valsalva and passive head movement did not trigger episodes. The patient described a compulsive urge to stretch to relieve a numbness sensation in her chest, shoulders, and head, which she sought rather than resisted.

Extracranial and transcranial color-coded duplex sonography at rest was normal. During head rotation and declination tests, transcranial duplex revealed a reversal of flow with a holosystolic pattern in the right vertebral artery V4 segment when the head was turned 45° to the left (supine and sitting), and a milder mirror-pattern in the left vertebral artery with right rotation. Upon return to neutral, flow normalized within 1–2 minutes, with gradual restoration of diastolic flow.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Epileptic seizures were considered given facial grimacing and limb twitching, but the EEG demonstrated slow-wave activity without epileptiform discharges — “EEG showed bursts of monomorphic, slow-wave activity (2–3 Hz), lasting from 3 to 12 seconds…predominantly frontotemporal and mainly ipsilateral to the side of the head tilt.”  
2. Cataplexy (narcoleptic episodes) was suspected, but sleep studies were normal and hypersomnia was excluded — “Daytime and nocturnal sleep features were unremarkable; a 5-naps Multiple Sleep Latency Test ruled out hypersomnia.”  
3. Extrinsic vertebral artery compression (vertebrobasilar insufficiency) was implicated by neck extension, supported by dynamic sonography — “The TCCS revealed a reversal of flow and holosystolic pattern in the V4 segment of the right vertebral artery…with the head turned to the left at a 45° declination angle.”  
4. Static vascular compressions or malformations were excluded by imaging studies — “We excluded static vascular compressions or malformations, abnormalities of the posterior fossa/craniovertebral junction, supernumerary ribs, and vascular conflicts at supra-aortic trunk emergence and course.”  
5. Vasodepressor faint was proposed in previous cases where systemic blood pressure dropped with diffuse cerebral dysfunction — “a drop in the systemic blood pressure followed by a diffuse cerebral dysfunction was recorded during the stretching maneuver in 4 other patients…suggesting a form of vasodepressor faint rather than a vertebrobasilar insufficiency.”  
6. Adrenergic dysfunction during Valsalva maneuver was also proposed as a contributing mechanism — “Adrenergic dysfunction during VM was also proposed as an additional factor.”
